front: In guided Emotional Inquiry, besides whether anything wants to protect or wants something to be different, what does Hudson have you notice?
back: Whether anything is being resisted.
extra: He asks this before you call up the feeling, after a minute of rest, with eyes closed. You answer silently.
source_title: The #1 Emotional Processing Technique For Anyone To Do

front: Try now, 2 minutes: call up a mild hard feeling. Poke it, breathe into it, hug it, then tell it to go away. What do you notice?
back: Notice how the feeling changes with each way you meet it. There is no right answer.
extra: In the last round of his guided audio, he also has you tickle it, chase it, listen to it as if it were the wisest person you ever met, refuse to listen, let it in fully, and block it. Safety: if you feel flooded, stop and rest. Trauma work needs a licensed therapist, not a recording.
source_title: The #1 Emotional Processing Technique For Anyone To Do

text: Hudson says any question about the felt sense of an emotion works, as long as the inquiry is truly {{c1::curious}} and has no {{c2::agenda}}.
extra: An agenda here means a wish to change or get rid of the feeling.
source_title: The #1 Emotional Processing Technique For Anyone To Do

front: With a very triggering emotion, what does Hudson say happens if you repeat the inquiry many times?
back: You start to feel excited when the feeling comes up, because you get to explore it again.
extra: He suggests going through the exercise many times for such an emotion.
source_title: The #1 Emotional Processing Technique For Anyone To Do

context: Every emotion is a young child
text: Hudson treats each emotion like a {{c1::young child}}: neglect or punish it and it acts out more; give it {{c2::attention}} and it settles back into love.
extra: He also warns that letting it run wild is no better than shutting it out.
source_title: How to actually feel your emotions

front: In Hudson's view, what is fear of sadness?
back: Sadness. If you are scared of feeling an emotion, you are already in it.
extra: The same holds for fear of anger (anger) and fear of shame (shame). Avoiding it does not protect you.
source_title: How to actually feel your emotions

text: Hudson pictures joy as the {{c1::matriarch}} of the emotions. She stays away from any home that turns her {{c2::children}} (the other feelings) away.
extra: So you cannot let in joy while you keep the hard feelings out.
source_title: How to actually feel your emotions

front: His story: what moment taught Hudson to take emotions seriously but not literally?
back: Giving unconditional love to his 3-year-old, who was yelling "I hate you, daddy."
extra: He says it took him decades to learn to take emotions seriously without believing them.
source_title: How to actually feel your emotions

front: What does Hudson say most to-do lists really are?
back: Your critical self-talk written down: a list of things the voice in your head says you have to do.
extra: Then you either feel controlled by the list or feel bad that you did not finish it.
source_title: Your To-Do List is Just Your Inner Critic on Paper

front: What do to-do lists usually leave out, according to Hudson?
back: How you will do each task, in a way you will enjoy.
extra: His image: tell a 3-year-old to brush their teeth and it may not happen. Say "let's brush our teeth together" and it is far more likely.
source_title: Your To-Do List is Just Your Inner Critic on Paper

front: What is Hudson's car image for efficiency?
back: A car that burns a gallon of gas to go one mile is not efficient, however fast it goes.
extra: Efficiency is how little energy the work takes. So the measure of an efficient day is whether you still have energy, and how much you enjoyed it.
source_title: Your To-Do List is Just Your Inner Critic on Paper

front: To the worry "if I only do what I enjoy, I will do nothing of value", what does Hudson answer?
back: People enjoy being of service, having an impact and feeling purpose. So enjoyment leads back to valuable work.
extra: His story: his daughter loved a summer helping mangroves in Panama. On a trip through Europe she told him she missed that sense of purpose.
source_title: Your To-Do List is Just Your Inner Critic on Paper

front: What two inner causes of stress does Hudson name, in place of too much to do?
back: Constant negative self-talk, so you are always under attack, and not feeling your emotions.
extra: He says we usually blame stress on outside things such as money or workload.
source_title: The Secret to Effortless Accomplishment | Joe Hudson

front: Besides anger, what two other ways of getting emotional AT someone does Hudson name?
back: Getting sad at them ("poor me") and getting scared at them ("I'm so worried about you"), to control them.
extra: He calls throwing an emotion at someone emotional abuse. Emotional fluidity means feeling all emotions without doing this.
source_title: The Secret to Effortless Accomplishment | Joe Hudson

front: You know you should exercise and you do not. What does Hudson say is going on, instead of "I'm bad"?
back: You do not get it yet. You get it in your head, but not yet in your heart or nervous system.
extra: He says change comes when it lands on all three levels.
source_title: The Secret to Effortless Accomplishment | Joe Hudson

front: How does Hudson answer someone who asks why they would ever want to feel a hard emotion?
back: He compares it to working out: it burns while you do it, and you do it because you feel better after.
extra: He says the first emotion you learn to welcome is the hardest. After that, patterns start to change.
source_title: The Secret to Effortless Accomplishment | Joe Hudson

front: His story: what two opposite ways did Hudson use to avoid feeling emotionally abandoned, and what did both cause?
back: Pushing people away ("I don't need you") and getting needy. Both made people abandon him.
extra: He traces the fear to his father's alcoholism. Once he could look forward to feeling abandoned, the pattern faded.
source_title: The Secret to Effortless Accomplishment | Joe Hudson

text: Hudson says the best English word for letting go is {{c1::receiving}}, because "letting go" and "surrender" sound like things you have to do.
extra: He cites the Zen question: how do you let go of a hot frying pan?
source_title: The Secret to Effortless Accomplishment | Joe Hudson

front: If you learned to avoid closeness because a parent smothered you, what does Hudson say the job in intimacy is?
back: To be fully yourself inside the closeness, not to lose yourself in it.
extra: As a child, pulling away was the only way to keep a sense of self. So closeness feels like losing yourself.
source_title: The Secret to Effortless Accomplishment | Joe Hudson

front: His story: what view of his mother's fear helped Hudson forgive her?
back: Seeing her fear as devotion: we are not scared for what we are not devoted to.
extra: He warns not to jump straight to forgiveness. You may need to feel your anger first.
source_title: The Secret to Effortless Accomplishment | Joe Hudson

front: What daily practice does Hudson give for a marriage, borrowed from sharing in 12-step rooms?
back: Say one vulnerable thing to your partner each day. Keep it small, for example "I don't want pasta tonight."
extra: As in a 12-step meeting, it feels very exposed the first time and much less by the 100th.
source_title: The Secret to Effortless Accomplishment | Joe Hudson

front: What does Hudson say stuck is, at its simplest?
back: An emotion, not a fact. We are stuck with gravity and do not feel stuck; we often feel stuck where we are not.
extra: He contrasts soldiers in muddy trenches who do not feel stuck with an office worker who does.
source_title: How To Get Unstuck

front: What two forms of stuck does Hudson tell apart?
back: Stuck on a problem (I cannot get to where I want to go) and trapped (I cannot get out of where I am).
extra: He says the trapped form almost always comes with a sense of an oppressor.
source_title: How To Get Unstuck

front: What childhood does Hudson link to feeling trapped again and again?
back: One with no-win situations: you could not be yourself and still please the adults, so freezing was the best strategy.
extra: Any move got you attacked, so staying still and hoping it passed made sense then.
source_title: How To Get Unstuck

front: What is the first question Hudson asks a client who says "I'm stuck"?
back: "Are you stuck, or do you feel stuck?"
extra: His co-host recalls this from a coaching session.
source_title: How To Get Unstuck

front: What does Hudson's team call the moment when a person cannot put their world back together?
back: The 404, as in "page not found".
extra: Their advice: do not build a new story yet; stay in not knowing a while. He says the longer you can rest there, the faster you integrate. Pushing for results slows the insight.
source_title: How To Get Unstuck

front: In Hudson's view, which feeling under feeling trapped does he move first?
back: Anger, the natural reaction to oppression.
extra: He says moving anger is the quickest way out of stuck for most people. Fear comes second, sometimes grief. Safety: move anger alone or with consent, never at a person, and stop if you feel flooded.
source_title: How To Get Unstuck
key: In Hudson's view, what two feelings sit under feeling trapped, and which does he move first?

front: What does Hudson say happens when you try hard to get out of a freeze?
back: You freeze more. Telling yourself "don't freeze" keeps you frozen.
extra: Instead, he suggests: "Oh, I'm frozen. I wonder when I'll thaw." Relax and watch, and you thaw sooner.
source_title: How To Get Unstuck

front: Try, the next time you freeze: double the freeze on purpose, then triple it. What happens?
back: Notice whether the stuckness wears itself out. Hudson says doing more of it stops the resistance that keeps it in place.
extra: For the nervous system he also names gentleness, which the person did not get as a child. Safety: if this brings up old trauma or you feel flooded, stop and get support from a therapist.
source_title: How To Get Unstuck

front: Feeling stuck often avoids losing love or being attacked. What does Hudson say you are already doing to yourself?
back: Removing love from yourself and attacking yourself, for example by not speaking your truth and beating yourself up.
extra: So the stuckness does not actually spare you what you fear.
source_title: How To Get Unstuck

front: Why, in Hudson's view, did we learn as children to attack ourselves?
back: It felt easier to attack ourselves first than to be attacked by someone else.
extra: He says the strategy fit at the time. The adult keeps it, and may pick a partner who fits it.
source_title: How To Get Unstuck

text: Hudson says trauma {{c1::pulls you back in time}}. A person who often feels stuck is reliving a childhood that is {{c2::no longer their reality}}.
extra: His image: a veteran in Cleveland hears a car backfire and is back in Fallujah. Part of healing is seeing you are not a kid anymore.
source_title: How To Get Unstuck

front: Why does Hudson say it is better to move fear with other people than alone?
back: Fear often comes from being alone. Moving it by yourself keeps you alone in it.
extra: He describes moving fear as shaking the body and making sounds, like a deer that escapes a mountain lion.
source_title: How To Get Unstuck

text: Hudson says people who solve the puzzle of always feeling stuck find that the only thing they were ever stuck with was their {{c1::thoughts}}.
source_title: How To Get Unstuck

front: After a change in yourself, why does Hudson call "Will it last?" a limiting belief?
back: It is anxiety posing as a thought. All learning ebbs and flows; you forget and relearn.
extra: Taking a dip as proof ("I've lost it") is a second limiting belief. Same with quitting a diet after one slice of cake.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: What does Hudson say he has never seen a startup fail from?
back: Lack of effort. So he says the more important things are your relationships and your decisions.
extra: He mentions a very successful investor client who works a few hours a week.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: In the self-reliance pattern, which feeling does Hudson say the person refuses to feel?
back: Helplessness. As a child with no one to care for them, feeling it seemed like death.
extra: The Golden Algorithm: grinding to avoid helplessness causes burnout and worse decisions, which makes you more helpless.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: Hudson: why can a self-reliant founder come to look forward to feeling helpless?
back: Because the feeling signals what to change.
extra: The three signals: you are not delegating well, you are not letting others help, and a false limit is narrowing your decisions.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: Try today: thank five people for something they did for you. What do you notice about asking for and taking help?
back: Notice what it is like to see how much others do for you. Hudson gives this to change a self-reliance pattern.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: Hudson: besides "every day", what belief makes people grind?
back: It is all up to me: no grace, and no help from others.
extra: He says the question "What do I tell myself every day?" is part of the grinding pattern.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight
key: A grinder asks "What do I tell myself every day?". Why does Hudson say the question is part of the pattern?

front: In Hudson's image of emotion as a hose, what does anger look like when it is unkinked, with no resistance or shame?
back: Determination and clarity, as in Martin Luther King or Gandhi.
extra: Kinked, it comes out as sarcasm, as "I'm not angry, just do the thing", or as rage. He says this is the other half of seeing emotions as messengers.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: Why does Hudson say many CEOs are constantly angry?
back: They feel alone in it, as if no one has their back, though thousands of staff try to please them.
extra: When they listen to the anger without shame, it shows a boundary or an inefficiency to fix.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: What two changes does Hudson say make a positive visualization more effective?
back: Feel the emotions of it going right, and picture it happening now, not in the future.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: How often does Hudson say to visualize the outcome you fear?
back: Until the fear is gone. How you do it matters more than reps: slow down and feel everything you do not want to feel.
extra: Founders, for example, picture the death of the company: layoffs, going broke. Then they stop acting from fear. Safety: if you feel flooded, stop and rest.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: His story: what do Hudson and his wife do when their marriage stops working?
back: They both grieve the relationship as if it is over and picture the divorce fully. Then they talk as themselves, not to save the marriage.
extra: Once the loss is lived through, they no longer need to walk on eggshells.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: Many founders fear being homeless. What thought experiment does Hudson use on this fear?
back: If you knew you would be homeless but happier than ever, how scared would you be? We fear the emotional experience, not the event.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: Try, the next time your body tenses (say, at a "Can we talk?" message): stop for 1 or 2 seconds and ask "What is it like to be me?"
back: Notice what is there. Then go on, even anxious. Hudson says this works by repetition, not insight.
extra: Do not try to control the anxiety; he says that makes more.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: His story: why does Hudson's nervous system fire when he is a minute late for a podcast?
back: His rigid German mother treated 5 minutes early as late, and he got in trouble.
extra: He uses it to show that the nervous system is trained by early life, not by the present facts.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: What is Hudson's factory image for avoiding conflict?
back: Someone shows you where the machine is about to break, and you say thanks and ignore it.
extra: He says conflict is where efficiency can be gained, in a business or a marriage.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: What two metrics does Hudson use to judge a company's health?
back: How quickly people have the hard conversation, and how quickly they resolve it.
extra: A yelling CEO and a conflict-avoidant CEO both fail these, in different ways.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: Sales are off. Instead of telling the person what to do, what does Hudson suggest you say?
back: "Sales are off. I need a plan. Please bring it to me tomorrow." Let them solve it for you.
extra: Solving it for them disempowers them. First, ask open questions to understand their side.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: In a hard conversation, how does Hudson suggest you speak about the problem?
back: Be vulnerable about where you are, for example "I feel we've lost trust, and that's hard for me." Do not make it all about them.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: "Why are you such a jerk?" versus "Oh, you're being a jerk." What difference does Hudson use these to show?
back: Your inner stance: calm acceptance versus fear and attack. He says it changes how the other person takes it.
extra: He calls the calm presence vagal authority, nervous-system authority, plus seeing that you are there to serve them.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: What hidden form of negative self-talk does Hudson name, besides attacks and "you've got to do this"?
back: Cheerleading: "You've got this, you can do it." It implies you need it, and so undermines you.
extra: His image: no one tells Michael Jordan "you can make the shot, Mike".
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: How can you tell a thought is negative self-talk, and what does Hudson say replaces it as it fades?
back: It repeats. As it fades you have far less thought, and what remains feels more like fresh ideas.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: What image does Hudson use for how most people listen to their inner critic?
back: A person in the crowd nodding along to the politician they hate most: "Yep, that's right."
extra: He says changing how you react to the voice works far better than changing the voice.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: Why does Hudson say inner work starts to feel exhausting?
back: You tell yourself you have to do all of it. Ask instead: what is one fun experiment I will run this week?
extra: He says meditation, for most people, is self-abuse: trying to manage themselves with no enjoyment.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: When does Hudson say you can do without self-awareness?
back: Only if you landed where your nature already fits and the world never changes. If you must change, skipping it hurts you.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: How long does Hudson say it often takes before people feel that inner work makes life better?
back: About two or three years. Before that, others often see the change before they do.
extra: Like working out: after that point, people ask why they would ever stop.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: What one-week experiment does Hudson suggest for grinders?
back: Do nothing you do not enjoy for a week. When you hit a task you must do, find a way to enjoy it.
extra: His story: stuck by a smelly bin he hated to empty, he had to learn to enjoy taking out the trash.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: Why does Hudson say positive emotions are the scariest ones for most people?
back: They break your identity the most. "Go be in bliss and find out where you are."
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: His story: what test for meaningful work did Hudson's daughter take from his story?
back: A "billion-dollar idea" is one you would not sell for a billion dollars.
extra: He and his wife would not sell their business for a billion dollars if they could never do it again. He says work done to win or be liked can build big firms, but not contentment.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: What split does Hudson see in many top performers he coaches?
back: They feel better than everyone and worse than everyone at once: capable on top, broken underneath.
extra: He puts this at perhaps 60 to 70% of them. In fast-paced firms, few of them second-guess themselves.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: Why does Hudson say framing change as experiments works better than goals?
back: The brain avoids repeating what felt like a failure. In an experiment you only learn, so you never fail.
extra: Example: one rejection stops the next sales call; one slice of cake ends the diet. He says people who kept iterating lost weight more often.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: His story: what happened on day three of Hudson's first silent Vipassana retreat?
back: An 8-second experience that he was one with everything and all was good.
extra: He became obsessed with finding it again. He later called his search for enlightenment "porn for perfectionism". When awakening came, it was no finish line.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight

front: His story: why does Hudson say he was not a great venture investor?
back: He needed to be needed. So he coached the CEOs, and word of his coaching spread.
extra: A great investor, he says, backs founders who do not need them at all.
source_title: Sam Altman's coach destroys your limiting beliefs for 86 minutes straight
